wrong: The event rule was wider than the forecast's own definition and was not on the page.

why: The rule was adopted after the data had been read, so a dated addendum states it and the original is kept beside it.

published: The event rule counted any hourly amount above zero or any present-weather entry, read on 704 scored periods (stated 14 percent in the 10 to 20 bin under 12 hours, happened 43.9 percent).
wrong: The rule was wider than the chance it is scored against. The National Weather Service states its chance for measurable precipitation of 0.01 inch or more, and the rule also counted a trace and light rain with no measured amount.
now: From 10 November the primary reading counts an event when the hourly reports inside the period sum to 0.01 inch or more. The original rule stays on the page beside it. At adoption the original read 12 of 18 cells above and the new rule reads 3 of 18 above.
why: Raised in the cold read of the page. Decided after the data and said so on the page.

published: The shipped Bluesky numbers were built by uncommitted code.
wrong: bsky_tick.py carried an uncommitted change over the earlier commit. It adds beside notes and a longer bench note. It changes no rule or outcome.
now: The code was committed as it ran.
why: The commit on record has to be the commit that made the page.

published: The page linked /social/bluesky.json.
wrong: No publish entry existed for the file, so the link would have been dead.
now: A publish entry publishes /social/bluesky.json.
why: Every data link on the page must answer.

published: The Bluesky readings were built from a replay that stopped short of the live head.
wrong: After a reboot the replay stopped at sequence 24,946,605 (about 28 November 2025). About 20.8 million sequence numbers were missing, so 2025 was incomplete.
now: The replay was resumed and read to the live head at sequence 45,785,475. 42,743 sampled signatures passed. No rule, code or window changed.
why: The plan commits to a replay to the live head.

published: The temporary suspensions row printed 0 in the first reading. The page did not say gore sits beside graphic-media. The sampling was described as drawn at random.
wrong: A reader could take 0 as no suspensions in the stream. The stream serves 9,468 suspension negations dated 2025. The gore count (164) was in the data file and not on the page. The sample is chosen by a fixed hash.
now: The page explains the 0 and the 9,468 negations, shows gore beside graphic-media, and says the sample is drawn by a fixed hash of the sequence number.
why: The copy has to describe what the data show.

published: The API said each answer carries the time it was read, but read_at was the time of the request.
wrong: read_at was the request time, not the data's read time.
now: read_at is the time the data was read, as ISO UTC. served_at is the time of the answer.
why: The stamp now means what the page says.

published: The all-figures row combined World Bank figures read against 142 releases with UIS figures read against two years of API releases.
wrong: 5,069 of the 5,093 no-release figures are UIS, so the row read as mostly unmatched.
now: A note beside the row says the history lengths differ and that most no-release figures are UIS.
why: The combined row could mislead without the note.

published: The draft said a figure matching an older release is a copy of that release.
wrong: A match shows the figure carries the release value. It does not show where the figure was copied from.
now: The page says the figure carries that release value and names no cause for any gap.
why: Provenance cannot be read from a match.

published: Eleven governing-document quotes. Four stopped mid-sentence without an ellipsis. The 3,565 ft entry was labelled 5.1.A.1 and 5.1.B.1. Sections 2.D.1.b and 2.D.1.c were said to govern calendar year 2026.
wrong: Only 2.D.1.a governed 2026. The 3,565 quote was 5.1.B.1 only. The heading left out the Drought Contingency Plan and Minutes 323 and 330.
now: The cut quotes end in "...". 3,565 ft quotes 5.1.A.1 in full. 2.D.1.b and 2.D.1.c say in force through 2026 and 2.D.1.a says governed calendar year 2026. The list is retitled to its two documents and names the DCP and Minutes 323 and 330.
why: Quotes and labels must match the documents.

published: The page said the rows were every projection of the latest measured month, that every row is in the full record, that plan, code and trend history are public, and that it is read about every half hour. One table was titled other reservoirs but listed Mead and Powell.
wrong: The code shows leads 0 to 12 only. No rows file was published. The desk kept no history file. The scheduled read was not yet on the scheduler.
now: The rows are described as projections made 0 to 12 months ahead. The full-record and trend history lines are dropped until true. The table is titled Reservoir storage against stated capacity. A history file now grows on each run.
why: Copy must be true when read.

published: The page left out items the plan promised: the 6.0 maf rows, the inverted-band count, the Most Probable outside its band count, the misread rate and the Most Probable lead 6 cells in the headline. It also gave one overall misread rate of 0.3 percent.
wrong: The misread rate is 1.0 percent (8 of 790 months) for 2000 to 2005 reports and 0.12 to 0.39 percent later. 115 band rows are inverted and 16 of 86 Mead and 10 of 85 Powell bands at lead 0 are zero wide.
now: The page shows the 6.0 maf rows apart, the inverted and zero-width counts, the outside-band count, the misread rate by era, and the Most Probable lead 6 cells in the headline. No cause is named.
why: The plan said these would be shown.

published: The plan and page described CONSISTENT as a possible outcome.
wrong: With about 20 water years a 95% interval is about 0.33 wide. A band cell needs about 61 water years and a Most Probable cell about 96 to fit inside its zone.
now: The page says no cell can read consistent at this sample size. The desk reads a miss or cannot tell.
why: The page promised an outcome the data cannot give.

published: Lake Powell six months ahead was inside the band in 49 of 82 issue months with 25 below.
wrong: The reader missed the Lake Powell table in the August 2020 Probable Minimum report, whose heading is scanned as "Powell" or "Lake Powe ll". All 24 Powell rows from that band month read cannot tell.
now: The reader matches those headings. Lake Powell reads 49 of 83 with 8 above and 26 below. 22 Powell band cells gain one row. No outcome changes.
why: A readable table was missed on the stated side.

published: The headline read Lake Powell six months ahead BELOW on the plan ruler, 95% Wilson on water years, interval 38.7 to 78.1 percent.
wrong: Weighting water years by row count or pairing them reads cannot tell, upper bounds 80.8 and 78.7 or 81.8 percent. The water-year ruler also treats neighbouring water years as independent and they are correlated at long leads.
now: The plan outcome stands. Three after-data rulers print beside it, labelled added after the data, and the page says Lake Powell depends on the ruler. Lake Mead reads below on every ruler, upper bounds 61.1 to 78.7 percent.
why: The plan ruler is not conservative and the headline did not say so.

published: The page compared 34 of 96 cells reading above or below with about 5 expected by chance.
wrong: The chance cutoff assumes 96 independent cells. Each lake 24 band cells reuse the same 86 issue months. The flagged count also moves with the ruler: 34, 28 or 19.
now: The chance comparison is gone. The page lists the flagged cells by lake, test and lead and says neighbouring cells share reports and target months.
why: The cells are not separate results.

published: The headline and page called the 80 percent probability that an elevation falls inside the Minimum to Maximum range "our reading of the inflow probabilities Reclamation states".
wrong: Reclamation prints the 80 percent sentence about elevation on page 1 of 182 of 205 Minimum and Maximum reports, 79 of 86 band months in both. The plan copied only the catalog blurb.
now: The headline quotes Reclamation's sentence. "Our reading" stays only for the Most Probable median test. Plan Addendum 2 records the sentence and the seven band months without it. No rule or threshold changed.
why: The page attributed a stated figure to us.

published: The page did not show where the two Reclamation measured series disagree.
wrong: HDB monthly and the Lower Colorado end-of-month table differ for Lake Mead in 9 months since 1990, for example 2002-06 (1159.19 against 1160.19). Scoring uses HDB as planned.
now: The page shows the measured-side cross-checks.
why: The plan said they would be reported.

published: The headline carried no interval and the Most Probable interval column did not say how many water years it was counted on.
wrong: Intervals must say what they are.
now: The headline carries its 95% intervals counted on water years (Mead 29.9 to 70.1 percent, Powell 38.7 to 78.1 percent) and the column says on how many water years.
why: Every interval says what it is.

published: The live panel said "Elevations in feet above sea level" and called USGS 09379900 a separate gauge and datum.
wrong: RISE gives Lake Mead datum as the USGS 1912 Power House Datum, add 0.55 foot for NGVD 1929. The data fit a different gauge and do not establish a different datum.
now: The datum notes quote RISE.
why: The wording was looser than the source.

published: The live panel showed the largest 1, 2 and 7 day rise in 60 days and a lowest-since-December-1999 line.
wrong: They were added after the plan and not labelled.
now: They are labelled added after the plan.
why: Readings made after the plan must say so.

published: The plan listed the reading done before it was sealed.
wrong: Before the seal we also read the full Lake Mead daily history from 1935 and the narrative pages of the October 2026 study. Neither set a projection against a measured month.
now: Plan Addendum 2 adds both reads to the disclosure.
why: The disclosure must list every read made before the seal.

published: The desk summary said the October study had Mead 15.5 ft above where it ended, 11 elevations, and a lowest daily reading since 1938.
wrong: The 15.47 ft is the April 2026 Probable Minimum gap. The Most Probable was 17.78 ft above. It is 10 elevations and one provision with no elevation. The reading is lowest since December 1999, the start of the record read.
now: The April 2026 Lake Mead row reads 17.78 ft below the Most Probable and 15.47 ft below the Probable Minimum, each named. The page keeps lowest since December 1999.
why: The summary was not carried into the ledger or any post.

published: The live feed stamped its update time with the year after the month.
wrong: The freshness watcher could not parse it and would have read the feed as unreachable.
now: The stamp is YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM in UTC.
why: A stale feed must be detectable.

published: The sealed plan said table values were read by eye.
wrong: The values were read directly from the page text.
now: The plan says read directly from the page text. The wording edit is recorded in the seal file as a wording edit with no rule changed.
why: The plan should describe what was done.

published: The draft headline said about two thirds more cells would have been inside at 80 percent.
wrong: The arithmetic gives 66 of 83 and 66 of 82.
now: The headline says about 66 of each.
why: The number must match the arithmetic.

published: A second reading of the day check, defined after the data, was added beside the committed outcome using TikTok's published daily totals.
wrong: The committed day check failed on 11 February 2026 and on 30 September to 2 October 2026. All EU rows of the last three quarters were cannot tell.
now: The second reading replaces the day check in its own column and never in place of the committed outcome. Committed outcomes are unchanged.
why: The outcome rule is unchanged and the widening is labelled.

published: The lead said 25% of release cycles stated as supported had already stopped releasing (127 of 516).
wrong: The rule is no release in more than a year. The page says unreleased is not abandoned.
now: The lead says 25% of release cycles stated as supported had no release in more than a year (127 of 516).
why: The wording was stronger than the rule.

published: The HSTS test read 38 of 189, 20.1 percent, 15.0 to 26.4, ABOVE.
wrong: The reader followed redirects and stored the header of the final response, often on another host. The preload rule is about the base domain's own response. Of 189 rows, 125 were read after a redirect.
now: The reader follows no redirect. On 9 Nov the test reads 20 of 144, 13.9 percent, 9.2 to 20.5, CANNOT_TELL.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: Revision values were read from a Philadelphia Fed file.
wrong: The pages carry no reuse terms.
now: Values are read from the BLS tables and flat file. In the counted windows two values differ: April 2020 first estimate and February 2020 third estimate. The third-release window moves to August 2016 to August 2026. Both sources give 13 of 120 months moved by more than 122 thousand at the third release.
why: Source terms.

published: The issued bill QIA-2026-001 (23 October 2026) quotes IBM's real-time benchmarking tutorial in rows 3, 4, 5 and 9.
wrong: IBM revised the tutorial after we read it, so the quotes no longer match the live page. The bill did not say when the tutorial was read.
now: On 9 November 2026 one sentence was added to the bill's method line saying the tutorial was read on 22 October 2026 and has since been revised. An issued bill is not edited, so on 10 November 2026 the bill was restored to its issued text. The read date and the archived copy are on the QIA page rows instead. No figure, row or outcome on the bill changed at any point.
why: A reader following the quote today would find different text.

published: The 29 Oct release headline said IBM processors delivered more gate error than IBM states on every run.
wrong: The body limits it to the gate-error runs we made on 23 and 24 October.
now: The headline says IBM processors delivered more gate error than IBM states in every run we made on 23 and 24 October.
why: A headline wider than its body.

published: Rows Q3, Q4, Q5 and Q9 and the bill quoted an IBM tutorial sentence that the linked page no longer holds.
wrong: The page now redirects to a revised tutorial that does not contain the sentence.
now: The rows keep the quote with its read date of 22 Oct 2026 and link an archived copy and the current page. The issued bill is not changed.
why: A quote must carry the date it was read.

published: The new samples were read by a reader that kept no cookies.
wrong: A site that sets a cookie and sends the reader back to the same address read as a redirect loop.
now: Each read keeps its own cookie jar for the length of that read. The 12 trial reads are set aside and read again in the main pass.
why: Found in a 12-address trial pass before the main pass.

published: Step 1 filed 18 domains as blocked or server error (HTTP 308).
wrong: The reader did not follow an HTTP 308 redirect, which is a redirect and not a block.
now: Every address opens through a reader that follows 308. Every domain filed under a 3xx status was read again.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: Outcome series were read from FRED.
wrong: FRED terms restrict commercial use and bar storing its content in a database or archive.
now: Outcomes are read from BEA, BLS and the Federal Reserve Board. All 59 outcomes match FRED to within 1e-13. The target range matches on 6,535 of 6,537 days.
why: FRED terms of use.

published: Actions on notices were compared with statements labelled Article 16 or trusted flagger, and many notice rows read ABOVE.
wrong: The report counts actions per notice or per item and the database files one statement per decision. On 11 rows the database holds more notice-labelled statements than the report says items were notified.
now: Notice rows now take the larger of the actions and the notified items as the stated upper edge. The database band runs from zero to every statement the platform filed. Only X Jul to Dec 2025 notices still reads BELOW. 28 rows changed to cannot tell.
why: The two filings label notice sources differently, so a gap on these rows does not show a difference in what was removed.

published: The staged DSA rows compared YouTube, Google Maps and Google Play reports with all statements in the database. YouTube all measures read ABOVE 1.158 [1.153, 1.162].
wrong: These three services publish ads moderation in separate Ads template files. The report side dropped those files and the database side counted ads statements. For YouTube about 93% of the database statements are ads.
now: The main rows compare the report with statements not flagged as ads. Ads are read on their own rows against the Ads files. YouTube all measures reads BELOW in both halves (0.089 and 0.081). Google Maps Jul to Dec 2025 reads CONSISTENT. 15 rows changed.
why: The two sides did not count the same set of statements.

published: After the first fixes, the ads and combined rows showed only that the row was defined after the data.
wrong: A reader could not see that these rows read cannot tell because of the column-sum bound alone and would read consistent without it. The combined-row line on the Meta note was incomplete.
now: 26 rows (3 combined, 23 ads) show the reading without the column-sum bound and name the addendum. The Meta line says the combined row also reads cannot tell, and why.
why: Disclosure of the rule that moves a reading.

published: Addendum 5 set a lower edge from the largest restriction column only for TikTok, X and Snapchat, because their notes say TOTAL is a column sum.
wrong: Sheet 6 TOTAL equals the sum of columns H to U in 38 of 45 reports, so the same logic holds for most platforms. The trigger by note was not even.
now: The bound is applied by arithmetic to every report where TOTAL equals the column sum. Rows for Instagram and Pinterest own and own terms and conditions moved to cannot tell.
why: The same rule has to apply to every platform.

published: Platform notes were applied to some rows and not to others. Snapchat notices read ABOVE (593 times and 424 times). Facebook and Instagram rows ignored Meta's note on combined actions.
wrong: Addendum 4 covered notes of one kind for some platforms only. Snapchat's note says user reports were moved to own initiative. Meta's note says some actions are counted for Facebook and Instagram combined.
now: The rule is applied to every note that fits it. The Meta per-service rows read cannot tell. A combined Facebook and Instagram row was added and also reads cannot tell. Notes with no effect are listed in the plan.
why: Uneven use of a rule leaves some gaps standing and removes others.

published: The staged copy gave one reason for BELOW rows, named one unsized difference, and said the totals match on every day but three.
wrong: Other differences the reports show were not named. The daily match is within 0.05%, not exact. The read date printed in UTC without a zone. Some reason strings joined rules with semicolons. Edge ratios could print on the line.
now: The BELOW and ABOVE reasons name every difference neither side sizes. The page says within 0.05% on every day but three. Dates print in HST. Five figures print near an edge.
why: The copy has to say what the data show.

published: Rows read ABOVE or BELOW on very small margins, for example Snapchat Jan to Jun 2026 own illegal ABOVE on 1 statement against a stated 0.
wrong: The agreement band was purely relative. Several rows were decided by fewer than 100 statements.
now: ABOVE or BELOW must clear its edge by at least 100 statements. Otherwise the row reads cannot tell. The page says above needs at least 100 statements when the stated figure is zero.
why: A decision on a handful of statements is within the noise of filing.

published: The page did not say that the checks committed with the plan had failed.
wrong: Two of the four checks committed with the plan failed. Under the plan as committed every row reads cannot tell. A gated build also ran before two addenda were written.
now: The page says under the plan as committed every row would read cannot tell, and that both failures were located before reading the comparisons. The plan records the earlier gated build.
why: A reader needs to see what the plan as written would have produced.

published: Split rows (solely or not automated, own illegal or own terms and conditions) read ABOVE in one half and BELOW in the other for the same platform.
wrong: The two filings label the same decisions differently. Opposite readings in two halves point to a label difference, not to missing or extra statements.
now: These pairs read cannot tell with the reason that the two filings label the split differently. The counts stay on a row of their own. Rows that do not depend on labels (all measures, own as sheets 5 plus 6) keep their readings. 28 rows changed.
why: A split reading depends on how each filing labels a decision.

published: X rows counted only statements under the name X.
wrong: 1,469 statements under the name X (formerly Twitter) have the same profile and were not mapped.
now: They are counted as X. X Jul to Dec 2025 goes from 216,372 to 217,841 and no outcome moves.
why: Names must map completely.

published: Rows where sheet 8 is built from sheet 5 and 6 totals that are column sums still read their ratio, for example Amazon Jan to Jun 2026 all measures BELOW.
wrong: Sheet 8 can inherit a column-sum total, so the stated lower edge is too high. The referee named this a judgment call.
now: Addendum 6.5 gives sheet 8 the same lower edge. Amazon Jan to Jun 2026 all measures and not automated moved from BELOW to cannot tell. 24 rows in all moved, including 19 ads rows.
why: The rule was written before the rows it moves were computed and applied to every report alike.

published: Addendum 5 set a lower edge from the largest restriction column for three platforms, defined after the data.
wrong: A TOTAL that is a sum over columns can count one decision more than once.
now: The stated band runs from the largest restriction column to the stated TOTAL for those rows. The outcome the plan rule gives is kept on the row.
why: A decision appears at most once in each column, so the largest column bounds the count from below.

published: Addendum 4 set a rule from platform notes, defined after the data. BELOW and CONSISTENT became cannot tell where a note says the stated figure can exceed the database count.
wrong: Platform notes say some fields count items the database does not hold as separate statements, or leave out things it holds. The plan's bands did not carry these.
now: The rule is in the plan, marked defined after the data. The rule's own outcome is kept on each row and the platform's words are quoted. 10 rows moved to cannot tell.
why: Notes from the platforms show a difference in what each side counts.

published: The NOW page showed a Darkwave clock block from 1 Nov under the line that every line below is read from a live feed and moves on its own.
wrong: The block was last written on 1 Nov and later fires were on the Darkwave page.
now: The block carries the date of the fire it holds. A script now rewrites the feed after each fire from the plan own reading.
why: A stale reading was shown as live.

published: The method counted monitors that have a sensor meeting all four targets. The lead said 95% of 147 EPA monitors have a sensor within 200 metres that misses a target, with no window.
wrong: The code takes for each monitor its median-error sensor. The 95% is the June to September 2025 read.
now: The method matches the code. The lead says 95% of 147 monitors had a median sensor within 200 metres that missed a target, 1 June to 29 September 2025, and 45% with the humidity correction.
why: The rule and the window were not stated as the code ran them.

published: The lead said 5 of 13 airlines now schedule each route longer against flown time than a year ago.
wrong: The reading is a median over routes, and the share 5 of 13 reads cannot tell. Each route read as every route.
now: The lead says 5 of 13 airlines widened the gap between scheduled and flown time on their median route, January to August 2026 against 2025.
why: The claim is about the median route.

published: The page copy said committees report each payment to Google, and used the term Nothing returned without a definition.
wrong: The itemization rule means payments under 200 dollars a year to a payee are not itemized. The intro promised per-quarter figures that were not published. Other sentences hid a sort key or an unexplained limit.
now: The copy states the itemization rule and the 400 dollar bound, defines Nothing returned, states the Above-side limits, links the slim public cycle file and drops the per-quarter claim.
why: Every sentence has to match what the data and the rule show.

published: Rows kept their outcome while other facts could change the reading, such as card payments larger than the gap, ad purposes labelled not candidate-specific, and a related advertiser in the window.
wrong: Below has shields for money paid to others and unseen money. Above had none. Eight Below rows had card payments or reimbursements larger than the gap less the size.
now: These rows carry a flag and keep their outcome: 8 for card payments or reimbursements, 5 for purpose text, 1 for a related advertiser. The page states the Above-side limits.
why: A reader should see what could change the reading.

published: Above rows rested on Schedule E amounts that the filer marked as estimates in 24 and 48 hour reports.
wrong: Four Above rows fail once those estimates are removed from the lower edge, among them Gun Rights America 2020 and 2022 and For Our Future 2024.
now: Rows with ESTIMAT in the purpose count in the upper edge and not the lower. A row that reads Above or Consistent only with them reads cannot tell.
why: An estimate is not a payment.

published: 19 of 49 Above rows read Above where Google states no spend in the window, so the floor alone decided them.
wrong: The outcome followed from a 1,000 dollar floor with no Google spend to compare.
now: Above needs Google spend stated in the window. Otherwise the row reads cannot tell. Above went from 49 to 28 across all cycles.
why: An Above reading needs a figure on both sides.

published: Nothing returned counted 170 cycle rows.
wrong: The test counted Google spend up to 98 days before the window and 31 days after it. 93 of the 170 rows have no Google spend inside the window. The page did not define the term.
now: Nothing returned needs Google spend inside the window and no FEC row or summary in that cycle. Run 7 has 24 rows. The page defines the term.
why: The plan's own definition was not what the code tested.

published: Below rows included committees matched to a Google advertiser by name, among them the House Republican Campaign Committee in three cycles and Greg for Montana 2020.
wrong: The Google advertiser was another entity, another account or another cycle's committee. Examples are a Michigan advertiser matched to a Minnesota committee and a 2022 candidate matched to a 2020 row.
now: A name match is set aside when Google lists the same name under a state registration, when two thirds of spend sits in another state, or when spend began more than 90 days before the committee's first filing. A name match cannot decide BELOW alone. A cycle guard and an empty-summary rule were added. 210 name matches were set aside.
why: Rules set after reading the rows, each one can only move a row out of a decided outcome.

published: The reader code added payee words and handled amendments differently from the plan text.
wrong: The reader added payee words and a YOU TUBE form, put every Schedule E Google row in the lower edge, and applied the amendment rule after filtering. Its comment said the patterns were verbatim from the plan.
now: Addendum 6 records the payee words and corrects the code comment. Mixed-payee Schedule E rows count in the upper edge only. The amendment rule runs first. Amended 24 and 48 hour entries are not counted twice. No outcome moved.
why: Plan and code have to agree.

published: Run 4 moved 34 CONSISTENT rows to cannot tell on unseen money of a few hundred to a few thousand dollars.
wrong: The itemization rule (11 CFR 104.3) caps how much unitemized money can be paid to one payee, so unseen money counts in full only for party committees or when less than 0.9 of operating disbursements is itemized.
now: Otherwise unseen counts as at most 400 dollars. Run 5 has CONSISTENT 26. The 0.9 threshold is ours and defined after the data. Rows whose outcome differs under the full rule are flagged.
why: The cap is set by the filing rule.

published: Run 3 had 99 BELOW and 41 CONSISTENT cycle rows.
wrong: Several BELOW rows rest on committees whose disbursements the itemized file barely holds. V-PAC 2026 shows 47,573,794 dollars in the summary and no itemized row.
now: BELOW and CONSISTENT must also clear the unseen money from the summary. BELOW went to 35 and CONSISTENT to 7. Run 3 files are kept.
why: A BELOW cannot rest on money we cannot see.

published: Run 2 had 7 quarter rows reading BELOW.
wrong: In all 7, Google states 0 to 5,800 dollars and the pool was negative from refunds. A negative pool is not an upper bound on money that reached Google.
now: The BELOW test counts positive items only. Run 2 cycle BELOW went from 103 to 99. Run 2 files are kept.
why: The plan says quarter rows can read only ABOVE or CANNOT_TELL.

published: Run 1 matched advertisers by committee ID and name only.
wrong: About 130 advertisers list a candidate ID or a lowercase committee ID. Name matching was also applied to advertisers with a state registration.
now: IDs are read case-insensitively and a candidate ID maps to its principal committee. Advertisers with a state registration are not matched by name. Run 1 files are kept as superseded.
why: Found after the first run printed its outcome counts and before any row was read.

published: The FaultsBench row for Fault 25 said the reply must give its width.
wrong: Under the plain wording the prompt does not ask for a width. The scorer checks that a width is given, not that it is right.
now: The row says a right figure with no width is scored a Fault, so this Fault is an omission, not a wrong answer.
why: A referee asked whether the scorer rejects correct answers and we ran controls.

published: The page gave the ibm_kingston clock reading of fire 8 as FINAL CONSISTENT without saying how it arose.
wrong: Each copy read cannot tell and the pooled copies were read as consistent. The unrounded lower bound is -0.04982 against the -0.05 margin and the earlier fire read the other way.
now: The page says how the label arose, prints the unrounded bound and the seed counts side by side (17 of 20 and 4 of 20), and discloses the inversion against the 31 Oct reading.
why: A label on the margin must show its step.

published: The IRIS lab page said YO Read, a paper reader, got run dates right on 0.818 to 0.892 of 148 held-out papers, against 0.520 for a keyword reader, and that it passed its plan.
wrong: YO Read had been given the wrong or a cut-down text for 22 of the 148 test papers. The code that turns notes into answers misread 5 data-link answers.
now: The score was held on 3 November and withdrawn on 4 November. A rescore under a rule fixed before it ran replaced it, and the page says the rescore was decided after the first scores were seen. YO Read is not in use.
why: The test was not built from the right texts.

published: Row Q1 gave the interval for the slope of measured against stated zz by pair only.
wrong: The by-triple interval reaches 0.00.
now: The row adds [0.00, 0.37] by triple and says the slope is far below 1 in every variant. It says IBM stated zz barely predicts the coupling we measured.
why: The claim is far below 1, never above 0.

published: Row Q9 said every change in the sampling null is larger than sampling alone gives, and marrakesh was about twice that.
wrong: The null at the real shot counts is fez 8.8%, kingston 9.8% and marrakesh 15.1% on 1/1024 records. One change sits at 1.6 times the null.
now: The row prints the null at real shot counts and names the thinnest margin: kingston, 22 Oct 02:16 to 08:55 EDT, 15.6% against 9.7% from sampling alone, 1.6 times.
why: The thinnest margin was folded into the word every.

published: The hourly panel text said readout counts used 1,024 shots on ibm_fez and ibm_marrakesh and 4,096 elsewhere.
wrong: The first four marrakesh runs of 30 October, 02:12 to 05:22 UTC, were re-read at 4,096 because their records were not all on the 1/1024 grid. The re-read call count was not printed.
now: The text says the count is read from each run record. Across the 24 runs the readout calls went from 1,043 to 754 and 289 of them (28%) withdrew to consistent. None changed direction.
why: A referee check of the re-read found the shot count claim and the call count missing.

published: Several Zenodo entries were labelled Read: Full text.
wrong: For these records we read the record page only. The record holds no PDF or the paper is inside a zip that was not opened. Two codes had no support.
now: The entries say Record page only, or Record page and a third-party errata only. Two unsupported codes are dropped. One later version dated 2 Nov 2026 is noted.
why: The read label must say what was opened.

published: The List entry for Zenodo 20367012 carried an F4 item that run dates are not printed.
wrong: The paper prints the run date as 23 January 2026 on ibm torino.
now: The run-date item is removed. F4 stays on the missing raw counts.
why: An author wrote about the F4 items and we read the paper again.

published: The List entry for UniMind showed code F6 with no basis line.
wrong: The entry did not say what the code rested on or that the author had answered.
now: The entry says Table XII gives 450 trials per cell while two cells fit 167/205 and 85/93. The author confirmed both counts on 2 Nov 2026 and says v1.8 will add an n column and a corrected caption.
why: The author wrote in and confirmed our recount.

published: The Darkwave Correction Kit version 1.0 was published as a kit that adds the virtual-Z correction after a mid-circuit readout.
wrong: On its first hardware fire on ibm_kingston the kit read like the study code but its correction gave back 0.264 [0.248, 0.285] of the turn, below the 0.5 the rule needs. Version 1.0 merged readouts separated by barriers into one group.
now: The page shows the failed first fire and version 1.1, which starts a new group whenever a qubit is read again. In the second fire the correction gave back 1.012 [0.993, 1.027] and the kit passed.
why: The kit was tested under preregistered plans and the first result was a failure.

published: The entry for arXiv 2509.18259 said the estimated circuit duration in Supplementary Fig. 2 was about 330 to 390 us, that CZs alone take at least 606 us, and that the published values match the noiseless model.
wrong: Our digitisation gave 320 to 370 us. The CZ time is 606 to 638 us over 50 walks. Relaxation at the plotted durations adds 0.02 to 0.11 and the published values sit within 0.004 of the noiseless model.
now: The entry gives 320 to 370 us, 606 to 638 us over 50 walks, labels the main-text counts as arXiv v1 and prints relaxation at the plotted durations and at the printed gate times.
why: A check of the shipped entry found the digitised range and the relaxation estimate were not measured the way the entry said.

published: The plan note for the clock fires said every label is unchanged after the 20,000-draw rerun.
wrong: That check compared numbers and cut the labels off. At 20,000 draws the first ibm_kingston clock reading goes from FINAL CONSISTENT to CANNOT_TELL, and its table comparison goes from BELOW to CANNOT_TELL.
now: A dated correction to the plan note states both label changes. The page had printed the clock reading as cannot tell since 31 Oct.
why: The plan note stated something the check did not show.

published: The headline counted each model by its latest pair of passes.
wrong: A model that changed on one pass and was the same on the next left the headline. Three such models were not shown anywhere.
now: Descriptive additions with no outcome: models that changed on any pass with an interval, a table of every pass and each change with files added, removed and replaced.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The headline said 22% of ClinicalTrials.gov trials past their results deadline have posted no results (4,881 of 22,316).
wrong: The registry does not store whether a trial is an applicable clinical trial or whether a delay was certified. The reading was cannot tell, so past the deadline was not established.
now: The headline says 22% of trials of FDA-regulated drugs and devices that reached primary completion at least 13 months ago have no results posted (4,881 of 22,316).
why: The page can say what the registry holds and not what the law requires.

published: The page said 13 months ago and that ten records of the first stopped-trial test were read in full.
wrong: The window ends 14 months before the read month. The ten records were not opened before the first read. They were opened on 30 Oct and all ten had one lead sponsor, which holds 24 of the 25 records of the test.
now: The page says 14 months before the read, lists the ten and names the sponsor concentration, labels the six added reason classes and says which kind of cannot tell each row is.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: time.ntp.se and time.sidn.nl read as servers that returned nothing.
wrong: Neither name resolves (NXDOMAIN, 48 of 48 queries failed). The second seat column also used the reference seat bound and the page named a cause for the shared offset.
now: Both names are removed and listed as retired. The second seat prints its own half-delay and bound. The page names no cause.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: Every table printed the outcome above for a silent share (24.3% [16.9%, 32.8%]) with no rule.
wrong: The page never said above what.
now: The body states the rule: above when the lower end is over 10 percent, consistent when the upper end is under 5 percent, otherwise cannot tell.
why: A reader needs the threshold to read the label.

published: The page listed 35 of 37 HSTS mismatches.
wrong: Two rows, epicgames.com and wp.com, had not been opened when the page was published.
now: Both were read again with a second tool and are listed. The page shows how many mismatches wait for a read in full.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The outcome was shown on the interval over months only.
wrong: At the 30 Oct read the same rule on the interval over calendar years gives cannot tell for both counts, where the interval over months gives consistent for the third release and above for the benchmarked value.
now: The page shows the outcome the same rule gives for the interval over years. It is descriptive and was defined after the first read.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The row said their marrakesh multiplier of 1.91x brackets our figure.
wrong: The authors do not print 1.91x for marrakesh. It is our ratio 0.0063 over 0.0033, and 1.91x is their kingston multiplier.
now: The row states the ratio as ours, 1.91 (0.82 to 2.45), and keeps the 36x figure, not about 600.
why: Our ratio was attributed to the authors.

published: The row said scores moved z by up to 47.
wrong: The row mixed a shift with its significance. Scores moved up to 0.43, which is up to 47 shot-noise widths. The audit left the cause open and "hardware change" named one.
now: The row gives scores moved by up to 0.43, up to 47 shot-noise widths, with no cause named.
why: A shift and its significance are different quantities.

published: The row said the factors close 23 to 75% of the simulation-to-hardware gap, and quoted "promising" from the abstract.
wrong: The word is in the Discussion. The 23 to 75% mixes point values at the low end with the top of the CZ interval at the high end.
now: The row names ibm_pittsburgh and the factors applied one at a time and drops the combined range.
why: The range mixed two rulers.

published: The row asked whether the simulator was noisy.
wrong: The paper states the simulator is ideal and noiseless. Its own counts put 9.5% of shots outside the two allowed states, so that statement is what fails.
now: The row says the simulator is called noiseless but its counts put 9.5% of shots outside the two allowed states.
why: The check read the paper wrong and the fault was in the statement.

published: The row said an infidelity of 5.0 against the stated median.
wrong: The 5.0 mixed the 21 Oct stated median with a factor taken against the 23 Oct record. On one record it is 4.3.
now: The row says 4.3 infidelity.
why: Both figures must come from the same record.

published: The row said standalone PEC at d = 6 was not run and gave 3.6x.
wrong: It ran and did not converge. The paper prints 3.7x.
now: The row says it ran but did not converge and gives 3.7x.
why: The paper and the run record both disagreed with the row.

published: The row said a 132-sigma figure could not be rebuilt.
wrong: It rebuilds to 132.7 from their raw shots when the null width is used. With the width in their own script it is 93.7.
now: The row states which width the 132.76 uses and gives both values.
why: The claim of non-reproduction was wrong.

published: The row said measured signals are 2.6 to 4.4 times below what stated errors predict, and that the paper damps structure by about 3x.
wrong: Neither figure could be traced, recomputed or recounted.
now: The row keeps our traced ibm_kingston factor of 1.30 to 1.37 and says the damping against stated errors is not measured here.
why: Untraceable figures were pulled.

published: The row said 14 of 17 reproduce.
wrong: The count is 15 of 18.
now: The row says 15 of 18.
why: The recount from the cached table gave 15 of 18.

published: The row said the factor accounts for 42 to 74% of the twofold gap, at the factor medians.
wrong: The 42 to 74% belongs to the factor intervals 1.19 to 1.34. At the factor medians it is 54 to 59%.
now: The row gives 54 to 59% at the medians and 42 to 74% across the intervals.
why: Each range must state the ruler that produced it.

published: The row said classical runs of the same problem take 6.4 s and 9.7 s against about 90 M attempts per second.
wrong: Neither figure is in any kept file. The kept record says 0.07 to 0.87 s at 67 to 91 M attempts per second.
now: The row gives 67 to 91 M attempts per second and converged ln Z in 0.07 to 0.87 s on three instances of the same class.
why: A number we cannot trace to a file does not stay on the page.

published: The row gave -2.55 for a quantity the text prints as 2.54.
wrong: The recount differs from the printed figure.
now: The row prints 2.54 as the paper does.
why: The row now matches the printed value.

published: The row said the run sat at 1.19 times the prediction from IBM stated figures and 0.77 times the prediction from the other model.
wrong: The two ratios cannot be traced because the script that produced them was not kept.
now: The row gives 0.137 per cycle (fidelity 0.872) and the stated figures. It says no ratio is printed because the script was not kept.
why: A ratio without its script cannot be rechecked.

published: The row said the cos(8 phi) model is consistent at 5%.
wrong: The test used the wrong degrees of freedom. At their df of 4 it gives p 0.074, and at df 3, which counts the two fitted parameters, it gives 0.036.
now: The row states both p values and drops the consistent label.
why: The label rested on the wrong df.

published: The row gave an upper bound of 6 to 30 test samples for the accuracy steps.
wrong: Only the minimum sizes 6 and 32 follow from the paper. The upper bound cannot be derived.
now: The row names the 6, 12, 18 or more and 32, 64 or more sample cases with their accuracies.
why: A bound we cannot derive was cut.

published: The row gave 120 +- 40, 95% [41, 199] against exact 240, and put our resilience 0 reading beside their resilience 2 figure without saying so. It coded the finding Q17, a gate-error cause.
wrong: The interval [41, 199] assumes no correlation between two moments and the worst case is [12, 228]. The run measured no gate error, so Q17 named a cause it did not test.
now: The row prints both intervals with their levels, says +- 40 is one standard error, states resilience 0 against their 2, and uses code F3.
why: The wider interval is the one to use when correlation is unknown.

published: The row read the sign of a result as resting on "-0.0010 +- 0.0007 (1.4 sigma)".
wrong: The 0.0007 was the trivial-circuit column of the record table, not an error bar.
now: The row gives 0.13 sigma at the record's own 1/sqrt(16384).
why: The wrong column was read as the uncertainty.

published: The row said to treat the result as a property of the chip in September, not of the circuit, and gave one chain phase sign change since September (+46.3 to -46.8).
wrong: On 29 Oct the same chain read -9.3 +- 3.8. The run ruled out the circuit as the only cause. It did not show a chip property.
now: The row says the finding was absent on 24 Oct at 0.0126 [0.0115, 0.0138] (99%), 1.3 times stated, with the 29 Oct repeat. It names no cause.
why: A number that moved by 37 degrees in five days cannot carry a stated cause.

published: The Braket row B4 said running neighbours at the same time adds crosstalk, so the simultaneous figure is expected at or below the isolated one.
wrong: No source states this and we did not measure it. A mechanism was written as an expectation.
now: The row says the simultaneous figure is stated above the isolated figure on these 7 qubits. No mechanism is named.
why: The audit holds only the seven pairs.

published: The chain lookup listed readings from a chain entry that a later entry had corrected, with no mark.
wrong: Entry 9 was corrected by entry 10 and 57 of its 83 readings were not in the correction. The lookup still showed them as current.
now: An entry named by a later correction is marked superseded and leaves the lookup. It stays in the whole-chain table.
why: A corrected reading should not be shown beside current ones.

published: The same line gave a CZ range built from interval ends (1.21 to 1.39) beside a single-qubit range built from medians (1.31 to 1.37).
wrong: One sentence used two different rulers for the two gates.
now: Both gates use the medians of our three kingston sessions. The line says the factors close 17 to 20% of the N=9 gap and widen the N=2 gap by about 2%.
why: A range is only comparable across gates if it is built the same way.

published: The QIA calibration runs on ibm_fez and ibm_marrakesh gave IBM's readout figures an interval as if each came from 4,096 shots.
wrong: Every readout figure in those records is a multiple of 1/1024, so the figures come from about 1,024 shots. Their intervals were drawn half as wide as they are.
now: The shot count is read from the record of each run. Every earlier fez and marrakesh run was re-read and each correction added to the chain. Across the 24 runs the readout calls went from 1,043 to 754. 289 of them withdrew to consistent. None changed direction and no T1 call changed.
why: The interval has to match the shots behind IBM's figure.

published: The correlations page said +0.0012 +- 0.0024 at zero wait is nothing, that balanced reruns killed both fakes, and that entanglement itself costs nothing extra.
wrong: The reversed arm reaches both 0 and +0.0124 within one standard error. The two balanced runs differ by less than two standard errors. A consistent reading is not a proof of no effect.
now: The page says consistent with zero and cannot tell. It says the imbalance is not shown to be the cause. It defines the +- as one standard error across pairs.
why: The wording claimed more than the intervals support.

published: The Hahn page said twelve runs on six processors and that the marrakesh fresh-record run waits for IBM to remeasure.
wrong: A thirteenth run existed. The marrakesh fresh-record run reads CONSISTENT under both fits, so marrakesh does not meet the rule.
now: The page lists thirteen runs. Marrakesh fresh run reads 1.015 [0.937, 1.130] and 0.958 [0.902, 1.016], both consistent. The marrakesh range is 0.907 to 1.015 and 0.892 to 0.958.
why: A finished run was missing from the table.

published: The Washington State row quoted a memo ending at a finding of not responsible.
wrong: The memo continues that the finding was because AI detection was submitted independent of any other supporting evidence. The bin label also said without numbers over a quote that prints 33%.
now: The quote is finished and the bin reads Outcome reported without counts.
why: The cut removed the stated reason.

published: The UMN row said effect consensus on 42 of 65 statements and evidence consensus on 0 of 65.
wrong: The report says 42 of 65 learning processes reached consensus. The 0 of 65 is not in the report.
now: The row says learning processes and states that the 0 of 65 is our count from the report evidence tables under its own 75% rule.
why: Our count was shown as the report finding.

published: The page said final grade -0.32 to -0.37 SD for the UMD study and that 41 instructors and 3,387 students registered.
wrong: The paper gives 0.37 SD in the abstract and 0.27 to 0.37 in the text. The -0.32 is our division of its Table 3. The 41 and 3,387 are from the pre-registration and the paper analyses 30 and 2,379.
now: The row gives the paper figures, marks the -0.32 and -0.37 as our division of Table 3, and gives both pairs of counts.
why: Our arithmetic was shown as the paper result.

published: The Public AI policy cell for MIT and Cornell read None found.
wrong: Both institutions have a public committee report.
now: MIT and Cornell read Found with a link. None found stays only on our own row and is dated 25 Oct 2026.
why: The cell read an absence that the record contradicts.

published: The page said 0 of 148 colleges and universities have published a measured learning outcome.
wrong: The list has 148 rows and one is our own. So 147 are colleges and universities.
now: The page says the list has 148 rows, one of them ours, and the counts include our own.
why: The denominator included our own row.

published: Four vendor-statement rows read as an outcome that covered the whole sentence: FU1, KV1, KV2 and Y4.
wrong: Part of each quoted sentence was untested or mismatched. FU1 names no scenario and Offline is +47.2% while Server is +62.3%.
now: The four rows read cannot tell with the tested and untested parts in the note.
why: The one-word outcome claimed more than the check covered.

published: Five vendor-statement rows read BELOW where the file shows more than the statement. They included RR12 (18.218 against 18.02), AR2 (88 and 96 against 87 and 94) and BV1 (34301.9 against 34301).
wrong: The page defines ABOVE as the file showing more than the statement. These rows showed more, or showed both directions.
now: RR12, AR2, BV1 and GV2 read ABOVE. RR19 reads cannot tell because one count is above and one below.
why: The outcome word must follow the definition printed on the page.

published: The Apple M3 row showed a description that belonged to another source.
wrong: The shared id M3 was Dell MI355X. The Apple description is the 40-core GPU line.
now: The Apple M3 row reads 40-core GPU in quotation marks. Each source owns its ids.
why: Only M3 of the shared ids was wrong.

published: The plan addenda for rounds S1 to S3 gave a commit time of about 11:30 UTC for the outcome step and a run stop at about 01:05.
wrong: The addenda were committed at 11:07:51 UTC and the outcome files at 11:12:36 UTC. The run stop was about 00:58 UTC.
now: Dated correction lines carry the commit times. The original lines are untouched.
why: The order of plan and outcome is a published claim and it needs the commit record.

published: Rounds S1 to S3 counted every chat and plain variant of the card tasks.
wrong: Reading 10 replies per variant in full showed parser faults. In S1 the GSM8K chat strict-match missed 4 of 10 and the BBH plain variant scored 0 on four correct answers because of a leading space.
now: A variant with more than 1 of 10 replies misread is tagged cannot tell (parser) and no longer counted. No row outcome changed.
why: The same rule is applied to S2 and S3 so the three rounds agree.

published: Round S2 said plain variants and chat flexible-extract read 10 of 10 replies as written, and chat strict-match missed 2 correct answers in 10.
wrong: The chat flexible-extract took the wrong number on question 8, so 9 of 10. Chat strict-match found no answer on 5 of 10.
now: The row prints 9 of 10 for chat flexible-extract and 5 of 10 for strict-match with two correct. The outcome stays cannot tell.
why: Reading the replies in full disagreed with the printed count.

published: A heading over the papers table said the papers check out.
wrong: The rows used a post-hoc rule and unreleased keys.
now: The heading names what the table shows.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: Gone was 69 of 1,980 links (3.5 percent).
wrong: Abstracts copy LaTeX escapes into addresses. Five links carried a backslash, were asked in that form and counted as gone.
now: Gone is 65 of 1,980 links (3.3 percent). The lead says papers read and, of them, those with a link (3,960 and 1,868).
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The snapshots held launches as watched.
wrong: The first snapshots already held 100 launches that had flown before being watched, and none can be scored.
now: The feed counts launches watched before they flew apart from those already flown at the first read. The page says so.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The training section pooled 99 sessions and said 92 of 99 had their lowest validation loss before the last check.
wrong: Until 26 August the validation step scored a random 100 of 489 examples each time, so a low loss before the last check is expected and says little about training.
now: The page splits the sessions: before the fix 90 sessions (36 improved, 85 with the lowest loss before the last check), after 9 (0 and 7).
why: The pooled figure hid a change in how validation was scored.

published: The finalists section said the selection rule and the reading rule were committed before any round was read.
wrong: The scorer plan was amended after rates were computed and the finalists were chosen on the rescored rounds. The page showed only the plain-prompt arm.
now: The note says the scorer plan was amended 11 times, nine of them after rates had been computed, and that only the plain-prompt arm is shown.
why: The page now says what was and was not fixed before the rounds were read.

published: The Falcon section said training finished and gave a gain table without saying how many training runs stood behind it.
wrong: The table is one training run per arm, one seed. A second seed and two further evaluation sets had been run and were not on the page.
now: The section says one training run per model and one seed, and that a second seed and two further sets have been run and are not shown yet.
why: One seed can change which items the adapter gets right.

published: The page said that with seeds as the unit MapSteal leads on 2 of 18 settings, not the 12 of 18 the means give.
wrong: The 2 of 18 is not separated from chance over 18 tests and the 12 of 18 is a correct count of means. The wording read as a correction of the authors.
now: The page says it resolves in 2 of 18 settings, uncorrected for 18 tests, consistent with zero in 15 and behind in 1. It says the authors 12 of 18 is a correct count of means.
why: The reading is stated with its multiple-test caveat.

published: The page said 800 of 800 items identical on the same host and 0.95% of 8,000 items change on a different GPU.
wrong: One sentence used two units for items. 800 is questions and 8,000 is question-position cells.
now: The page says 8,000 of 8,000 question-position cells identical and 76 of 8,000 cells (0.95%) change, A40 against A10G. The primacy gap is +0.0019 [-0.0050, +0.0088], consistent with zero.
why: Both counts must use the same unit.

published: The Key put the share of verdicts that flip for three frontier judges (31.0%, 31.3%, 30.9%) beside our own flip rates.
wrong: Ours is net of the exact repeat. The judge figures come from an earlier experiment, run once per judge with no repeat floor.
now: The Key says the judge figures are a different measure and gives the pinned October figure +12.5 [8.0, 16.7] above its floor.
why: Unlike rulers sat in one sentence.

published: The top table gave rates of answers that changed when the prompt was reworded for falcon3:3b (22.2%), smollm2:1.7b (30.0%), granite3.3:2b (29.4%) and phi4-mini (10.6%).
wrong: The rates rested on 27, 20, 51 and 142 of 200 items because the rest of the replies could not be read.
now: Each cell prints k of 200 items. A model with more than 10% unread reads cannot tell, so these four no longer show a rate.
why: A rate over a small readable share is not a reading.

published: The finalists section said the two models with the lowest Fault rate under the Guard wording were smollm2:1.7b and qwen3:4b.
wrong: qwen3:4b had no readable cell. The selection code skipped only some cannot-tell outcomes, so it kept a model with no score.
now: The selection rule excludes every cannot-tell outcome. The finalists are smollm2:1.7b and olmo2:7b. A dated addendum to the plan records the change.
why: The written rule gives a different pair than the code ran.

published: IRIS said the judge saw 24 items more than once and gave differing verdicts on 22 of them.
wrong: The 24 were 2 adapter names, 16 one-character buckets and 6 chance collisions of a short log label. The label is not an item id, so the 22 is not a count of items judged twice.
now: Both figures are withdrawn. They say nothing about the judge's agreement with itself.
why: The count grouped log labels, not items.

published: Step 2 read 13 of 500.
wrong: The reader took the mrf-url value only up to the first space, so two hospitals with spaces in the file name read as 404.
now: Step 2 is 11 of 500. All 511 domains were read again and five addresses differed.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The top line and table title said endpoints below 100 percent uptime.
wrong: The plan counts endpoints with a status other than 0 or a 5-minute uptime below 100. The list was also cut to 60 rows while the count was left whole.
now: Labels say flagged by OpenRouter or below 100 percent, the table shows the status and one-decimal uptimes, and the list is not cut.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: Guards item 25 carried the figure four times in five for a second reviewer that rejects deliberate faults.
wrong: No record holds the figure.
now: The figure is removed. The sentence says the reviewer inverted both of its verdicts.
why: A figure with no record does not stay.

published: Counts above the table: 1,053 fetched period rows, 347 scored rows and a chance floor of 113 rows with 0 events.
wrong: The counts were rows, while the cells hold each period once and read only stated chances with a lead of 0 to 48 hours.
now: Counts come from the same set as the cells. The chance floor is 26 distinct periods with 1 event.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: Faults 20 said the two-answer failure comes from compression and is not a knowledge failure.
wrong: The record gives cold 44 of 77 and seated 81 of 295. It cannot separate context from the other differences between the arms.
now: The entry gives both rates with counts and says we cannot tell whether context reduces the rate. The compression claim is removed.
why: The record does not name a cause.

published: Faults 41 and the Guards headline said discipline does not improve and the corrections changed the rate not at all.
wrong: Per 1,000 words each day is within one width of the day before. Day 3 against days 1 and 2 pooled is 1.24 times the rate, exact 95% interval 0.76 to 1.99. That interval includes no change and also a fall of up to 24%.
now: Both documents say each day is within one width and give the rate ratio and its interval. They say a fall of more than 24% is outside the interval.
why: A flat reading was stated as a proof of no effect.

published: Faults entry 24 said the replies per reply read 27.3%, 27.4% and 47.4%, a collapse on the third day at +3.02 widths, and per thousand words nothing happened.
wrong: The two readings used different numerators. Pushbacks were counted per reply and frames per thousand words.
now: On one numerator, frames, the entry says per reply 27.3% to 22.6% to 39.5% (9 of 33, 42 of 186, 30 of 76), above the second day at +2.64 widths. Per thousand words it is consistent at +0.97 widths.
why: The lesson holds on one numerator.

published: Whitepaper statement RV6 said 45 of 4,000 blocks read have a second paid coinbase output, and read below.
wrong: The 45 rows are failed coinbase reads with no output, not payouts. No recent block has a second paid output.
now: The check counts blocks with two or more paid outputs and lists unread coinbases apart. It reads cannot tell while unread blocks remain.
why: A failed read was counted as an extra payout.

published: The first reading held 281 vendor rows.
wrong: The reader skipped dates with a three-letter month and dates with a non-breaking hyphen, so 41 OpenAI rows were missing, among them 12 shutdowns inside the next 60 days. It also read OpenAI Date and Update rows that describe other events as shutdown dates.
now: The reader handles both forms. In those tables only a row that says it will shut down carries a shutdown date. The store holds 322 rows.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: Pages read as GONE, CHANGED or unreachable by our reader.
wrong: The full read was first done on 30 Oct. Two pages answering 404 to our reader open in a browser, one page did not open for the reader because of a missing intermediate certificate, and four CHANGED pages are viewer pages whose text cannot be compared.
now: The notes are in the full-read file and the viewer pages are classed by size alone.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: 146 or more institutions linked, counted at 159.
wrong: The rule counted the first cell of any table as an institution, so 13 of 159 were finding labels or headings.
now: The first cell counts only when the first column is headed Institution or School. The count is 146. Sources stay 297.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The page did not state the two-day floor, the date-only rule or when the series rule was decided.
wrong: The series rule was decided after the first portal read and the page did not say so.
now: The page states the floor, the date-only rule and that the series rule was decided after the first portal read.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The page said provider statements were quoted beside the rows. Shares showed 0 to 0 for a count of zero.
wrong: No statement has been collected, so none was quoted and no row has an outcome word. Zero counts hid their upper end.
now: The sentence is removed. Shares show one decimal, so 0 of 1,139 reads 0.0 with an upper end of 0.3.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The ATLAS electricity and carbon state tables counted Epoch AI's Google Papillion site (237 MW) in Kansas.
wrong: A city-and-ZIP geocoder fallback placed it in Kansas. Its Epoch address names Papillion, Nebraska.
now: The site is placed in Nebraska. Kansas loses 237 MW and Nebraska gains it on the electricity, carbon and cost-to-scale tables and on the map.
why: Each dot has to sit where its source address says.

published: The ATLAS electricity utility table listed an entry named Adjustment (EIA utility number 99999, Texas).
wrong: It is EIA's balancing line and not a utility. The page's own note under the providers table said so.
now: The entry is dropped from the utility table and its rows file.
why: The table lists utilities only.

published: A table of studies by month indexed.
wrong: It left out the 13 QIA studies that have no indexed date, so its rows did not add up to the studies read.
now: They are a row called month not recorded.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The June to September 2025 read was stated as 122 days.
wrong: The read used an end of 23:59:59 on 30 Sep 2025, so it holds 1 Jun to 29 Sep 2025, 121 of the 122 days stated.
now: The published result stands. Whether to read 30 Sep 2025 and score again is not decided.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The live panel showed sensor days and an hourly strip beside the monitors.
wrong: Each live sensor call asked for a window ending at 23:59:59, and the service returns only complete buckets, so each call lost its last day. Sensor days 28 and 29 Oct were empty from 29 Oct 18:51 UTC until 30 Oct 14:00 UTC and the hourly strip was empty in all 17 runs. AirNow hour files cached part filled were also used.
now: The window ends at the next midnight. A day is stored only when sensors return rows. The strip takes an hour only when its file holds at least 60 percent of the monitors. The panel shows the newest day it holds.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: The live display counted airports with a program now.
wrong: It counted every item of the FAA feed, closures included. The closures are notices to general aviation that can run for months and the feed prints their dates without a year.
now: The count covers delay programs, ground stops and general arrival and departure delays only. Closures show under their own heading.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: A table of published scores kept (systems read at least twice, number changed, share, outcome).
wrong: The table did not show on the page because the shared page reader treated a row holding an empty list as many rows.
now: The reader is fixed, the table shows and each system row links its Detailed Results report.
why: Found in the site pass.

published: A vendor disagreement needed two of three seats to fail.
wrong: The Mac and the Pi share a house network, so one home fault counted as two seats and as a vendor disagreement. The control floor of 0 misses in 170 rounds was not a zero rate.
now: The Mac and the Pi are one seat. The floor is the Wilson upper end, 0.022 at 170 rounds. BELOW needs at least two episodes.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The plan's known-good records NCT03515551 and NCT04537429.
wrong: The reader never ran them.
now: The reader reads both before publishing and publishes nothing if either reads otherwise.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: A reasons block with a bin called Other text.
wrong: The bin held 31 percent of the stopped records and a bin with no definition hides different reasons.
now: Six classes were added after seeing the data and labelled so. Unmatched texts are published.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk after seeing the first read.

published: time.apple.com read ABOVE on the runner seat from minus 4.72 against a 0.15 bound.
wrong: A constant that every server shares on a seat is the seat part, not the server part, and it was scored against each server's stated bound. The plan named the Mac as second seat when it is the GitHub runner network.
now: Each seat's common offset is removed before the second reading. The headline is the raw outcome only where the two agree, otherwise CANNOT_TELL.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The plan said a beacon previous-entry input is the entry before it.
wrong: It is the newest feeds entry. A qbits entry was written between them once (entries 22 and 23).
now: The verifier checks the real rule. The tape was not changed. The reader writes qbits entries before feeds.
why: Found on the first qbits entry.

published: A class called silent.
wrong: The word is on a list of words we do not use because a bin named silent hides different outcomes.
now: The class and page call it unreleased. The rule, counts and outcomes are unchanged.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The cycle-level interval was Wilson, treating cycles as independent.
wrong: Cycles inside one product are not independent. Neptune alone holds 22 of the 126 silent cycles.
now: The interval is a bootstrap over products (17.1 to 32.8 percent), with Wilson (21.0 to 28.4 percent) beside it. Two product-level shares were added and labelled as defined after the first read.
why: Found after the corrected read and before publication.

published: The first read reported about half of the tested cycles SILENT.
wrong: The code treated an end date of true as no end stated, so ended cycles such as Exchange 4.0 counted as SUPPORTED.
now: A state EOL_NO_DATE is counted apart and not tested. Only a date string counts as a stated end. The first numbers were never shown.
why: Found after the first read and before anything was published.

published: The QIA stability row, the queue row and the CADENCE row.
wrong: The stability row read NOTHING_RETURNED because of an expression error. The queue row kept only the last three processors. CADENCE appeared over two denominators.
now: The stability row shows its reading. The queue row shows every processor. CADENCE says 623 below of 1,254 readable series plus 205 that cannot tell.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The first table held only tests that report a share with an outcome.
wrong: Every other live page also measures something and leaving them out hid them.
now: FEDSEP is added and a second table lists every other live page with its reading and state.
why: The owner said the table did not hold every test.

published: The SPF count and a note that both tests read ABOVE.
wrong: The counter skipped an include it had already met, so it undercounted and was biased toward AGREE. The note was wrong: HSTS read ABOVE and SPF read CONSISTENT.
now: The counter follows RFC 7208. Every stored SPF record was counted again. Two domains changed class and no outcome changed.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The target list of pages the outside monitor probes.
wrong: The probe read the target list from one builder line that no longer holds the menu, so new pages were never added. It also reported /hermes/live.json unreachable, a false incident.
now: It reads every menu and desk entry. /hermes is skipped like the other division pages.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: Feed limits and incident counting for the outside monitor reading.
wrong: Feeds added after the plan took a default 40 hour limit, so a fast feed could be a day stale and read FRESH. One stale feed seen by three probes counted as three incidents. A reading stood for ever if probing stopped.
now: Limits are set from each read schedule. ABOVE needs three or more incidents in the last 24 probes. A newest probe over three hours old reads CANNOT_TELL.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: Wilson intervals over 120 months, and a note that every large month matched its archived release.
wrong: Consecutive months are not independent. Every large month printed the same full read note though only four months had been opened. The known-good asked for 24 months and the API gives 14.
now: A bootstrap interval over calendar years is shown beside it, defined after the first read. A month not read in full reads not yet read. The plan says 14 months and the code accepts 12 or more.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The calibration line for the Cauca study said our kingston gate factors, used as an upper bound in their twin, close about half of the N=9 gap and widen the N=2 gap by about 40%.
wrong: The about-half figure came from an earlier estimate and was never rechecked. Recomputed with the twin code it is 13 to 21% of the N=9 gap and about 2% at N=2.
now: The line says the factors close 13 to 21% of the N=9 gap and widen the N=2 gap by about 2%.
why: The recomputation with the saved twin code did not support the earlier figure.

published: Pip failures the classifier did not recognise read as DISAGREE.
wrong: A network or build error would have read as the project failing.
now: An unrecognised failure is not comparable with its message. No project changed class.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The second read: 545 agree, 0 disagree.
wrong: 22 of 545 AGREE rows were commands that do not install the project (the first pip install line in cffi installs pytest).
now: A command counts only when a target equals the project name. Otherwise it is not comparable. The result is 525 agree, 0 disagree, 475 not comparable.
why: Found by reading a sample of the AGREE rows in full.

published: The first read: 545 agree, 1 disagree, 454 not comparable.
wrong: The one disagreement was a placeholder (nvidia-cusparselt-cuXX) the reader did not recognise.
now: The placeholder rule covers XX, YOUR_ words and angle-bracketed words. The first read numbers are not used and the whole read was run again.
why: Found by reading the first read in full.

published: The page says it reads every paper in its categories.
wrong: When an arXiv request for a year and token returned nothing, the cell was marked done and never tried again, so the census could be silently incomplete.
now: A cell whose fetch failed is left not done, tried again on the next pass, and its failure is printed.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The page called the share a launch that slipped.
wrong: Slip is an absolute difference, so a launch a day early counted like one a day late. Cancelled or unflown launches were counted nowhere.
now: Each cell shows the signed median and counts of launches more than 24 hours later and earlier. The unflown count is stated as not yet fixed.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: 95 percent intervals on slip shares.
wrong: The interval function omitted a division, so published intervals were wider than the named Wilson interval.
now: The shared tested function is used. No scored launch existed yet, so no verdict changed.
why: Found on a read of the code.

published: Addendum 1 said choa.org was a reading error.
wrong: It was not. The address returns a gzip-compressed web page, decoded and read in full.
now: DISAGREE stands. Step 2 is 487 AGREE, 13 DISAGREE, 11 NOT_COMPARABLE.
why: Found by the full read of every DISAGREE row.

published: The first read: step 1 511 AGREE, 517 DISAGREE. Step 2 14 DISAGREE. Step 3 13 DISAGREE.
wrong: Five of ten fully read step 1 rows are not hospital websites in the sense of the rule. Eleven of 13 step 3 rows were reading errors (JSON and zip files).
now: Step 1 outcome is fixed as CANNOT_TELL because it is not a compliance rate. The reader decodes gzip and calls a page a web page only when the content starts as HTML. Step 3 returns not comparable for JSON and zip. Steps 2 and 3 were read again.
why: Found by reading rows of the first read in full.

published: NeoQuasar/Kronos-Tokenizer-2k was filed as DISAGREE at a ratio of 1,979, and a note said none of the 12 rows was a reading error.
wrong: The card says 2k is a context length, so the reader took it as 2,000 parameters. That row was a reading error. A failed list request could also publish 0 models.
now: The size token no longer accepts K. A list under 500 models stops the pass and keeps the last read.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The first read: 133 agree, 15 disagree.
wrong: A 1-bit packed repository was not on the packed list. Two repositories had a safetensors total that disagrees with their own dtype breakdown.
now: The packed list matches 1 to 8 bit widths. A repository whose total differs from its breakdown is not comparable and is listed apart. The first read numbers are not used.
why: Found by opening the 15 DISAGREE rows.

published: 352 models and 295 datasets read no license file in the repository root.
wrong: A failed file list call, or an empty list from a failed request, was scored as no license file.
now: A failed call is its own class, not comparable, with the reason file list could not be read. Stored no license file rows were read again once.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: Fhrozen/FSD50k was filed with the mismatch rows as a custom text.
wrong: Read in full, the file agrees with the tag cc-by-4.0. The reader did not find the words Creative Commons in the title region.
now: The title region reading also accepts Attribution followed by a version number and a CC BY notation. The whole read was run again.
why: Found by the full read of the two mismatch rows.

published: The second read found no DISAGREE rows.
wrong: One file read was an image because the matcher accepted any name starting with LICENSE.
now: The matcher accepts only no extension, .md, .txt and .rst. Two descriptive rows were added with no outcome. The whole read was run again.
why: Found while checking what the not comparable rule was hiding.

published: The first read: 82 models agree, 350 models and 330 datasets with no license file.
wrong: All 3 model disagreements were Creative Commons files read as CC0 because of a trailer phrase. All 330 datasets read no license file because the list endpoint returns no file names for datasets.
now: The Creative Commons family is read from the title region and dataset file names come from the per-dataset endpoint. The first read numbers are not used and the whole read was run again.
why: Found because the results looked wrong before they were believed.

published: Cells counted every stored row of a forecast period.
wrong: One period fetched twice in the same lead bin counted twice in that cell. That overstated n and made every interval too narrow.
now: A period (station and start time) counts once per cell, from its earliest fetch in that cell. Periods whose stated chance falls in a gap between bins are in no cell and are not scored.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: 95 percent intervals for each cell of the calibration table.
wrong: The interval function left out one division, so the intervals were wider than the Wilson interval the plan names. They were up to 38 percent wider at n = 10 and about 5 percent wider at n = 100.
now: The page uses the shared tested function and was republished.
why: Found on a read of the code while moving desks onto the shared code.

published: Triples with a missing median, range or outcome.
wrong: They were skipped with no count, and the full read opened only this-year misses. The plan reads Septembers from 2013 and the code starts at 2015.
now: They are counted with the reason. Next-year misses are listed as not yet read in full. The 2013 and 2014 pages carry no median, so those years are not comparable.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: A note said the two unemployment outcomes were recomputed from the BLS API.
wrong: They were not. The keyless BLS API returns only the last three years, so 2020 and 2021 are not in it.
now: The 2020 and 2021 outcomes are from FRED only. No row or rule changed.
why: Noticed when the note was checked.

published: The federal funds rate was scored against the fourth-quarter average of the effective rate.
wrong: The SEP median is a year-end level. The 2022 miss (median 4.4 against an average of 3.65) comes from the choice of basis and not from the projection.
