now: The main test is unchanged. A sensitivity row defined after the first read scores the rate against the year-end midpoint of the target range and is labelled so.
why: Found by the full read of the horizon 0 misses.

published: The page showed snapshots as fresh after a pass that stopped.
wrong: The fixture gate promised in the plan was never run, and a stopped pass still wrote and published a summary, so a stale snapshot looked fresh.
now: Every saved page must pass the fixture gate or the pass stops and publishes nothing. The page stamp is the time of the last completed pass.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The first notice table counted lifespan as notice for Google rows.
wrong: The parser put the Google release date column into the deprecation date field. Google states no deprecation date.
now: The notice table covers only rows that state a deprecation date. A second table gives stated lifespan for Google rows. The first snapshot was discarded and read again.
why: Found after the first snapshot and before anything was shown.

published: Age was described as the fetch time minus the modified date.
wrong: The code used the current clock, so every stored portal file grew older between reads and a dataset could move from CONSISTENT to BELOW with no new read. FEMA is also one of nine named portals and is not in the output.
now: Age is the portal file fetch time minus modified. The FEMA gap is stated on the page source list.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: 95 percent intervals on the share of series behind their cadence.
wrong: The interval function left out a division, so intervals were up to 38 percent wider at n = 10. The CDC behind share read 18 to 34 percent.
now: The shared tested function is used. The CDC interval is 19 to 33 percent. No outcome changed.
why: Found on a read of the code.

published: A resolver that answered none of its queries (dns0_eu, 1,075 timeouts) read as blocking 0 of 486 domains, 0 to 1 percent.
wrong: That read as a filter that blocks nothing. A timeout says something about our path or the resolver, not its filtering, and sat in the denominator as not blocked.
now: A query with no answer is counted apart as a timeout and is not in the denominator. A resolver with no answered query shows nothing returned with its timeout count.
why: Found in our own audit of the desk.

published: The first round flagged 2604.24289 as WITHDRAWN.
wrong: The arXiv comment withdraws one section and the paper stands. The detector matched the word anywhere in the comment, which is looser than the plan class.
now: The detector requires the abstract or comment to begin with a statement that the paper itself is withdrawn. All studies were read again.
why: Found after the first round and before anything was published.

published: The first plan had no STACK row for the airline reading.
wrong: The first read showed 5 airlines ABOVE in 2026 against 2025 and the plan had no row for the pooled count.
now: A pooled count (airlines ABOVE out of airlines compared) was added after the data and is labelled that way. It has no threshold, so its outcome prints as CANNOT_TELL.
why: Added after the first read was read in full.

published: MODEL statements AR5 (AMD, fourth round) and RO2 (Red Hat, first OpenShift on GH200) read cannot tell.
wrong: Rounds before v5.0 had not been read. Their system description files hold the answer.
now: Those rounds are read from the system description files. AR5 and RO2 read consistent.
why: The earlier rounds were readable.

published: Each record of a portal counted as its own dataset.
wrong: CMS lists every historical release as its own record and an archived release cannot be updated, so old snapshots would read overdue.
now: Records that share a landing page are one series, read through the newest record. Counts of records and series are both published.
why: Decided from the file structure after seeing counts and before any outcome was shown.

published: Guards said unaided catches stood +15.4 widths above the sealed 7.7% bar (148 of 608).
wrong: The width treated the bar of 2 of 26 as exact. Its exact 95% interval is 0.9% to 25.1%, which contains our 24.3%. A Fisher exact test gives p 0.033 one-sided and 0.058 two-sided.
now: The figure is withdrawn.
why: A bar counted on 26 items carries its own uncertainty.

published: A draft bill line read the top-ranked ibm_boston qubits by IBM's stated T2 against the bottom-ranked, a gap of -0.392 [-0.676, -0.155].
wrong: IBM's stated T2 is itself a noisy snapshot. Two kingston records differ with a log spread of 0.42. Ranking on it and dividing by it gives a gap of this size even when the stated value is unbiased. Our simulation covered fit and shot noise only.
now: The line was pulled from the bill before it was issued and reads cannot tell. The deciding test ranks by one record and judges against a second, independent record.
why: The rebuttal survived its test.

published: The draft bill's effect row 13 read ibm_fez coherence at 2 readouts as above zero by a copy-gap reading.
wrong: That reading was defined after the data. Under the committed rule the two copies disagree and the reading is cannot tell.
now: The issued bill says fez cannot tell at 2 readouts under the committed rule and consistent with zero at 4 and 8.
why: The committed rule decides the printed outcome.

published: A draft line of the bill read 11 of 14 ibm_marrakesh qubits above the bound for a stated readout error of zero, using a bound of 0 out of 4,096 shots.
wrong: That marrakesh session's figures are all multiples of 1/1024, so they come from about 1,024 shots. The 95% bound for 0 of 1,024 is 0.29%.
now: The issued bill uses the 0.29% bound. Read alone, 9 of 14 qubits are above it. Read with every qubit, 11 of 14 are above it in each of two jobs.
why: The bound has to match the shot count behind IBM's figure.

published: Draft bill lines said ibm_fez and ibm_phoenix edges that IBM states as zz 0.00 beat at kHz rates, read as a deviation from IBM's figure.
wrong: A stated 0.00 could be a placeholder rather than a measurement. IBM's earlier records give these same edges 2.9 to 17.5 kHz, which matches our readings.
now: The lines read as a record note. The record drops couplings that earlier records listed to 0.00 while the gates on those edges stay live.
why: The placeholder rebuttal was tested and the finding was restated to what the records show.

published: A draft line of the bill said IBM's stale flag sat on 2,431 error entries and that the oldest T2 shown was 158 days past its measurement.
wrong: Synthetic test records were counted with IBM's records, so the record count was 69 where it should have been 66.
now: The line was withdrawn before the bill was issued.
why: Only IBM's own records can carry a finding about IBM's records.

published: A draft line of the QIA-2026-001 bill said IBM's readout_error was not the documented average of its two parts on 160 of 5,543 entries that share one measurement date.
wrong: The count compared readout_error with only one of its two parts. It also counted synthetic test records that are not IBM records.
now: The line was withdrawn before the bill was issued. The issued bill's note 11 counts 153 measurements where readout_error is not the average of its parts, and in every one a part is older than readout_error.
why: The test did not compare what the documentation defines.

published: A draft reading said the coherence of untouched ibm_fez qubits fell below a model built from IBM's stated T2 and zz figures, -0.095 at 16 echo steps.
wrong: Hahn echo runs then read fez T2 at its stated value on four runs, and the gap grew with the number of echo pulses while the echo-off arm stayed flat. Pulse error and crosstalk were not ruled out.
now: The reading reads cannot tell. It is kept as a row and was never printed on the bill.
why: The model could not separate IBM's figures from our own pulse sequence.
